name: Question 15
worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{1-x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,⟹\,-\text{d}u=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{1-x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{1-x}}}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x=-{\int }_{\infty }^{1}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{1-x}}}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{e}^{-u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }[-{e}^{-u}]_{1}^{a} \\  & =\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}+\frac{1}{e}) \\  & =\frac{1}{e}-{lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{a\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/4ef3194e946aec805866202a5e0ad521291d71b1fabc2df68d6cb1a4d93da42b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-\sqrt{1-x}}}{2\sqrt{1-x}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{e}-{lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{a}} \\  & =\frac{1}{e}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$
